# Aura

> Aura is a compiled, statically typed programming language with Python-inspired syntax, deterministic ownership, native execution, and no garbage collector. Its current focus includes reliable applications, agents, and ML infrastructure; its long-term goal is a general-purpose systems language for every type of software, including operating systems and device drivers.

## Project

- [Aura](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura#readme): Aura is a compiled, statically typed programming language for reliable software. It pairs Python-inspired syntax with deterministic ownership, structured concurrency, typed failure, and native executables. It has no garbage collector.
- [Aura](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura): Aura is a compiled, statically typed language with familiar, indentation-based syntax. The compiler checks types, ownership, mutation, exhaustive matching, failure handling, and task boundaries. Programs build as native executables with deterministic cleanup and no garbage collector.
- [Why Aura](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/positioning): Aura 0.11.0 is a technical preview of a compiled, statically typed language for reliable software. It combines Python-inspired syntax, deterministic ownership, structured concurrency, typed failure, and native executables.
- [Downloads](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/downloads): Aura 0.11.0 is a technical preview. The compiler, command-line tools, editor extension, reference manual, and source all ship from the [Aura GitHub repository](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura).

## Install Aura

- [Install Aura](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/install): Aura 0.11 ships as a self-contained command-line tool with its own private native runtime. Pick the guide for the operating system where `aura` will run:
- [Install Aura On Linux](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/install/linux): The Aura 0.11 preview supports x86-64 Ubuntu 24.04 and compatible Linux distributions that use glibc. The release has no Linux ARM64 or musl archives.
- [Install Aura On macOS](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/install/macos): Aura publishes separate macOS 15 archives for Apple silicon and Intel Macs. The installer uses `uname` to pick the right one.
- [Install The VS Code Extension](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/install/vscode): The **Aura Programming Language** extension provides `.au` syntax highlighting, indentation, snippets, diagnostics, completion, hover, go-to-definition, and document symbols.
- [Install Aura On Windows With WSL](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/install/windows-wsl): Aura has no native Windows executable. On an x86-64 Windows 11 machine, you install and run the Linux release inside Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL 2) with Ubuntu 24.04. The CLI, compiler runtime, your projects, and the VS Code language server all run inside WSL 2.

## Language Manual

- [Aura Language Reference](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual): This Manual is the normative reference for the implemented Aura language and runtime. It covers the complete syntax, name and type rules, ownership, execution, module APIs, diagnostics, limits, and tool contracts, in enough detail to reconstruct the language accurately.
- [API Index](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/api-index): This page lists every public builtin constant, function, method, module type, and builtin enum that the manual documents. Each entry gives the exact signature and a one-line summary. The linked manual pages have the examples and full rules.
- [Assertions](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/assertions): An assertion states an invariant that must hold for execution to continue. Use assertions for programmer errors and internal consistency. Do not use them for recoverable input or protocol failures. When a caller should be able to handle the outcome, return a typed `Result`.
- [Bytes, Text Codecs, And SHA-256](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/bytes): This page covers byte data, UTF-8 conversion, byte search, hexadecimal and base64 codecs, and SHA-256 hashing.
- [Classes](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/classes): A class is a nominal product type. Each value holds a fixed set of named fields and exposes the class's methods. Ordinary classes are move types. A class declared `copy class` is a copy type.
- [CLI And Tooling](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/cli-and-tooling): The `aura` command checks, runs, builds, and inspects Aura programs. It also serves the editor tooling. This page lists each command and flag, its output, its exit status, and the native build cache behind `run` and `build`.
- [Closures](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/closures): A closure is a small callable value with an expression body, written `lambda parameters: expression`. Parameter types come from context. A zero-parameter lambda may infer its result type from its body. A lambda without a capture list captures by value. An explicit capture list names outer locals and requests shared, mutable, or owned access to each one, and it must be exhaustive.
- [Collections](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/collections): This page covers Aura's three generic owned collection types:
- [Concurrency](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/concurrency): This page covers Aura's lightweight tasks. A task runs on a scheduler with pinned workers. The surface includes structured task groups, task handles, queues, cancellation checks, sleeping, and typed waits on one or several sources.
- [Conformance](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/conformance): This page maps each part of the specification to the tests that cover it. It also defines what a conforming program and a conforming implementation must do.
- [Contracts](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/contracts): A contract states a rule of a function, loop, or class in the code itself. A `requires` clause says what a caller must provide, an `ensures` clause what the function promises back, and an `invariant` what stays true while a loop runs or while an object exists. Aura checks every clause each time it applies, in `aura run` and in built programs alike, and stops the program with `AU4009` when one is false.
- [Control-Plane Modules](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/control-plane): This page covers Aura 0.11's small, typed host and control-plane modules: `sys`, `path`, `json`, `toml`, `log`, `trace`, `metrics`, and `control`, plus a summary of the HTTP client. They are meant for service launchers, workers, evaluation harnesses, and agent infrastructure. They behave the same through `aura run` and in direct native binaries.
- [Current Limits](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/current-limits): This page lists what the Aura compiler, runtime, and tools do not implement today, and the fixed limits they enforce. Limits are grouped by area.
- [Diagnostics](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/diagnostics): A diagnostic is the compiler's report of a rejected program or a runtime trap. This page lists every diagnostic code, the fields a diagnostic carries, and how the CLI and the editor present it. Diagnostics are part of the language and tooling contract.
- [Docstrings And API Docs](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/docstrings): A docstring is a plain triple-quoted string that documents a declaration. This page covers where a docstring goes, how editors and `aura doc` present it, and the limits the compiler enforces.
- [Enums And Pattern Matching](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/enums-and-match): An enum is a nominal sum type. Each value holds exactly one declared variant. When that variant has payloads, the value holds one value for each payload position. A `match` evaluates its scrutinee once, selects the first matching arm, and binds payload values for that arm.
- [Execution Model](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/execution-model): This chapter defines the runtime behavior that `aura run` and built programs share. Aura checks source statically, lowers it, and runs it. Evaluation within one expression is deterministic. The scheduler controls concurrency, and external I/O depends on the host.
- [Expressions](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/expressions): This page defines Aura's expressions: the available forms, how they group, their precedence, their evaluation order, and their main static restrictions. An expression evaluates to a value.
- [Foreign Function Interface (FFI) v0](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/ffi): Aura FFI v0 calls a small, fixed subset of the platform C ABI. It is an unsafe package capability for binding trusted native symbols that the process has already loaded. It is not a general system for dynamic libraries, pointers, or callbacks.
- [Filesystem Module](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/filesystem): The `fs` module provides one-shot helpers for common file operations. It also provides `fs.File`, an owned resource for handle-based work.
- [Functions](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/functions): Functions are module-level declarations introduced by `def`. A function's callable contract applies at every call site. It fixes:
- [Generics And Traits](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/generics-and-traits): This page covers generic declarations, inference and explicit specialization, traits, implementations, and how Aura dispatches trait methods and operators.
- [Grammar](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/grammar): This chapter defines the complete source grammar of Aura 0.3. The grammar is normative once the lexer has formed tokens. [Static Semantics](/manual/static-semantics) defines the static restrictions the grammar does not express, such as types, visibility, ownership, exhaustiveness, valid receivers, and API-specific rules.
- [I/O Module](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/io): The `io` module covers standard input and output. It also defines `io.Error`, the error enum that the filesystem and networking APIs share.
- [JSON Module](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/json): The `json` module represents any JSON data as one recursive enum, `json.Value`. Parsing returns malformed or unsupported input as typed error data. Dumping produces one deterministic JSON string, or traps when the value cannot be serialized.
- [Language Specification](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/language-specification): This Manual is the normative specification of the implemented Aura 0.11 development language. It defines what a conforming implementation must provide:
- [Lexical Structure](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/lexical-structure): This chapter defines how Aura source text becomes tokens and indentation markers. It is normative for source spelling.
- [Math Module](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/math): The `math` module provides exact binary64 constants and scalar `float64` functions for rounding, powers, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometry. Every function input is `float64`. The module performs no implicit numeric conversion.
- [Names And Scopes](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/names-and-scopes): This page covers how Aura resolves names. Resolution is static and never falls back to dynamic lookup. A name denotes one of these:
- [Network Module](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/network): The `net` module provides networking resources that cooperate with Aura's task scheduler:
- [Numeric Arrays](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/numeric-arrays): `Array[T]` is Aura's owned, contiguous numeric container for the CPU. Use it for local preprocessing, postprocessing, evaluation, and batch-shaped numeric work. It is smaller than a general tensor framework:
- [Ownership And Borrowing](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/ownership-and-borrowing): This page covers how Aura statically tracks whether an operation copies, moves, shares, or mutates a value. The rules apply to local bindings, parameters, method receivers, fields, supported indexed operations, collection iteration, pattern matching, task starts, and resources.
- [Packages](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/packages): An Aura package is a directory that contains `Aura.toml` and a `src/` source root. The package graph determines module paths, dependency import prefixes, git revisions, and which directory owns `Aura.lock`.
- [Performance](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/performance): This page records Aura's performance measurements. Each one has an exact workload, pinned source commits, raw observations, and content hashes. The measurements guide engineering. They are not language semantic guarantees. The speed targets for native code are ratios to matching Rust programs. The [design record](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/architecture_docs/22-batch-7-design-checkpoint.md#targets) lists them.
- [Process Module](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/process): The `process` module runs child processes. By default it uses no shell. A command is an explicit `list[str]` argument vector, or argv. So `["/bin/echo", "hello world"]` runs one executable with one argument. Aura does not split strings or expand shell syntax.
- [Randomness Module](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/randomness): The `random` module keeps two kinds of randomness apart. A seeded `random.Rng` gives a reproducible pseudo-random stream. The `secure_*` functions draw unpredictable values from the operating system. Construct an explicitly seeded `random.Rng` when results must repeat. Use the `secure_*` functions only when results must be unpredictable.
- [Statements](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/statements): Statements introduce and update bindings, control execution, or evaluate an expression for its effects. This page defines when each statement is legal and what it does when it runs. The exact syntax is normative in [Grammar](/manual/grammar#suites-and-statements). Compile-time legality is normative in [Static Semantics](/manual/static-semantics). Runtime sequencing and cleanup are normative in [Execution Model](/manual/execution-model).
- [Static Semantics](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/static-semantics): Static semantics are the rules the compiler checks after parsing and module loading, and before MIR lowering or native code generation. MIR is the compiler's mid-level intermediate representation. A module is well typed only if every declaration, statement, expression, pattern, call, move, and borrow satisfies these rules.
- [Status And Compatibility](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/status-and-compatibility): Aura 0.11.0 is a technical preview. It is suitable for compiler and runtime evaluation, examples, and controlled experiments. It is not a production systems-language release, and it is not a security boundary for untrusted programs.
- [Tuples](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/tuples): A tuple is a fixed-size value that holds a known number of elements, each with its own type. Use tuples to return, pass, unpack, and pattern-match a small group of values. Tuples are not variable-size collections.
- [Types](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/manual/types): This page covers Aura's type system: scalars, unions, copy and move categories, builtin and user types, annotations, and casts. Aura is statically typed, so every expression has a type. Type annotations are part of the public shape of functions, fields, methods, and many empty literals.

## The Aura Programming Language

- [The Aura Programming Language](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book): This is a book about Aura, a compiled programming language that reads like Python. You write indented blocks, `def`, `class`, f-strings, and `for name in names`, much as you would in a Python file. The difference is what happens before your program runs: the compiler checks the type of every value, checks who owns each piece of data and who is only borrowing it, and checks that every failure your code can meet is handled somewhere. Then it either runs the program straight away or compiles it to a native executable with no runtime to install alongside it.
- [Foreword](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/foreword): Most people who write Python for a living have a story about the bug that only showed up in production. Maybe a function was handed `None` on a path nobody tested, or one part of the program was still reading a list while another part emptied it, or a network call failed, raised an exception nobody caught, and took a long-running worker down with it at three in the morning. None of these are exotic. They are what happens when a language lets you write code quickly and then asks you to find out at run time whether the pieces fit.
- [Getting started](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch01-00-getting-started): Before we can write any Aura, we need the tool that understands it. Aura ships as one command, `aura`, which checks, runs, builds, tests, and formats your code, and also powers the editor support. In this chapter we install it and write our first few programs. By the end you will have `aura` on your path, you will have run a program three different ways, and you will have a package with its own tests that you can open in an editor.
- [Installation](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch01-01-installation): The first step is to install `aura`. Aura ships as a single command-line tool together with a small native runtime that it links into the programs you build. There is no separate interpreter, package manager, or language server to install: the one `aura` binary does all of those jobs.
- [Hello, world](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch01-02-hello-world): Now that `aura` is installed, it's time for the program every language book starts with: one that prints `Hello, world!` to the screen. We will write it twice, once as a script and once with a `main` function, and then compile it to a native executable so that you can see both ways Aura runs code.
- [Hello, packages](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch01-03-hello-packages): A single `.au` file is enough for a small program, but most code grows past one file. It picks up helper modules, tests, and eventually dependencies on other people's code. Aura's answer to all of that is the *package*: a directory with a manifest called `Aura.toml` and a fixed layout that the `aura` commands understand. Let's create one, split our greeting into a module of its own, write tests for it, and set up an editor to work on it.
- [Programming a word counter](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch02-00-word-counter): Let's jump into Aura by writing a real program together. We will build a small command-line tool that reads text from standard input, counts how often each word appears, and prints the most common ones. By the end, you will be able to feed it any text file and get back something like this:
- [Common programming concepts](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch03-00-common-concepts): The word counter in the last chapter used a lot of Aura without stopping to explain it. This chapter slows down and goes through the pieces that nearly every program is built from: bindings, the basic data types, functions, comments, and control flow. None of these ideas is unique to Aura, and if you know Python, much of the syntax will look familiar. What is worth your time is the set of places where Aura's rules differ, and the reasons it chose them.
- [Bindings and mutability](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch03-01-bindings-and-mutability): A program needs somewhere to keep the values it is working with. In Aura you give a value a name by writing `name = value`, exactly as you would in Python. We call that a *binding*: the name is bound to the value. There is no `let`, `var`, or other keyword in front of it.
- [Data types](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch03-02-data-types): Every value in Aura has a type, and the compiler knows it before the program runs. That makes Aura a *statically typed* language. Most of the time you don't write the types yourself, because the compiler works them out from the values, but they are always there, and they decide what you can do with each value.
- [Functions](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch03-03-functions): You have been writing functions since Chapter 1: every program so far has had a `main`. Functions in Aura look almost exactly like Python functions. You declare one with `def`, give it a name in `snake_case`, list its parameters in parentheses, and write the body as an indented block. The difference is that the types are part of the declaration.
- [Comments and docstrings](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch03-04-comments-and-docstrings): Code is read far more often than it is written, and some of what a reader needs to know can't be expressed in the code itself: why a constant has the value it has, what a function promises, which input a strange-looking branch is there to handle. Aura gives you two tools for this, and both work the way they do in Python. Comments are notes for people reading the source. Docstrings are documentation attached to a declaration, which your editor and `aura doc` can show to people who never open the file.
- [Control flow](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch03-05-control-flow): Programs make decisions and repeat work. Aura's tools for both are the ones you know from Python: `if`, `elif`, and `else` for decisions, and `while` and `for` for loops, with `break` and `continue` to leave a loop early or skip ahead. What needs your attention is the handful of places where Aura is stricter than Python. Once we've seen those, we'll finish the temperature program with a function that prints a conversion table.
- [Understanding ownership](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership): Every program has to answer a question that most languages hide from you: when is a piece of memory finished with, and who gets to say so? Python answers it at run time. Each object carries a count of the references pointing at it, the interpreter frees the object when the count reaches zero, and a cycle collector sweeps up groups of objects that only point at each other. You never write any of that down, and you never have to think about it until a program uses too much memory, pauses at a bad moment, or holds a file open longer than you expected.
- [What is ownership](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership): Let's start with a Python program that surprises almost everyone the first time they meet it:
- [Shared and mutable access](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch04-02-shared-and-mutable-access): At the end of the last section, our `total` function took ownership of the list it added up. That was more than it needed. `total` only reads the numbers, and once it has given us the sum it has no further use for the list. Taking ownership forced the caller to give the list up or copy it first, and neither makes sense for a function that only looks.
- [Copies and slices](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch04-03-copies-and-slices): Borrowing covers most of what functions need, but sometimes you really do want two independent values. You want to keep yesterday's scores while you change today's, or keep a name in a list and also store it in a record. For those cases Aura makes copies, and it makes them only when you ask. Asking takes a different spelling for different types, and every copy has a cost that grows with the value, so both are worth knowing before you reach for one.
- [Using classes to structure data](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch05-00-classes): A program that tracks a book you're reading needs a few facts about it: a title, an author, a page count, and how far you've got. You can keep those in four separate bindings, and for a dozen lines that works. Once there are several books, or functions that need all four facts at once, loose bindings start to drift apart. Nothing in the code says that `pages` and `pages_read` describe the same book, and nothing stops a function from being handed the page count of one book and the progress of another.
- [Defining and building classes](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch05-01-defining-classes): A class declaration lists the fields every instance has, with a type for each. Here is a class for a book:
- [An example program using classes](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch05-02-example-program): To see what a class changes, let's write a small program the long way first. We want a reading tracker: given how many pages a book has and how many we've read, it tells us how far through we are. We'll start with separate bindings, move to a tuple, and end with a class, looking at what each version makes easy and what it leaves to chance.
- [Methods](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch05-03-methods): A *method* is a function declared inside a class body. It is called on an instance with a dot, as in `dune.read(50)`, and its first parameter is a *receiver* that names that instance. You've seen receivers briefly in [Chapter 4](/book/ch04-02-shared-and-mutable-access). Here we'll turn the reading tracker's free functions into methods and look at each form of receiver in turn.
- [Enums and pattern matching](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch06-00-enums-and-match): A class describes data where every part is present at once. A book always has a title, a page count, and a position. A lot of data has a different shape. A book on your shelf is unread, in progress, or finished: exactly one of the three, never two. A command typed into our reading tracker is "read some pages of this book" or "list the shelf" or "quit", and each kind carries different information. A search finds a result or finds nothing.
- [Defining an enum](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch06-01-defining-an-enum): Let's give each book in the tracker a status. The quick way is a string field, `status: str`, holding `"to-read"`, `"reading"`, or `"finished"`. That works until someone writes `"Reading"` or `"finshed"`. The compiler sees a `str` either way, and the mistake waits for whatever code compares `status == "finished"` and quietly gets `false`.
- [The `match` control flow construct](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch06-02-match): `match` compares a value against a series of *patterns* and runs the code for the first one that fits. If you've used Python 3.10's `match` statement, the shape will look familiar. The difference that matters is that Aura checks your patterns at compile time: a `match` over an enum must handle every variant, or the program doesn't compile.
- [`T | None` and concise matching](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch06-03-optional-values): Some functions don't always have an answer. Searching a shelf for a title might find it or might not. Stripping a prefix from a string only works if the prefix is there. In Python, such a function returns `None` when it has nothing to give, and the caller is supposed to check. When the caller forgets, the program carries on with a `None` until something tries to use it, and then fails with a `TypeError` or `AttributeError` somewhere else. Tony Hoare, who introduced null references in 1965, later called them his "billion-dollar mistake", and this is the reason.
- [Managing growing programs with modules and packages](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch07-00-modules-and-packages): Every program we have written so far fits in one file. That works for a while, and then it doesn't. The file gets long enough that you scroll past the class definitions to find `main`. Two unrelated helpers both want to be called `format`. A function you wrote for one program would be handy in the next one, and the only way to share it is to copy and paste. Python solves these problems with modules, packages, and `pip`, and Aura solves them with the same three ideas, held to stricter rules.
- [Modules and imports](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch07-01-modules-and-imports): Our program for this chapter keeps track of a reading list: which books are on it, how many pages each has, and how far through the list we are. Let's start a fresh package for it:
- [Visibility and private names](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch07-02-visibility): At the end of the last section, every field of `Book` was public because the compiler asked us to make it so. That got the program running, but it also means any module that imports `books` can build a `Book` with any values it likes and change those values whenever it wants. For a class with four plain fields that might seem harmless. Let's give `Book` a field where it isn't.
- [Packages, dependencies, and workspaces](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch07-03-packages-and-workspaces): Modules organize the code inside one program. Packages are how programs share code with each other. Our `report.progress` module draws a text progress bar, and nothing about it is specific to books: a download tool, a test runner, or a backup script could all use it. Copying the file into each of those projects would work until the day we fix a bug in one copy and forget the others. A package lets us write it once and depend on it from anywhere.
- [Common collections](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch08-00-collections): Most of the data a program handles comes in groups: the lines of a file, the scores of a class, the words in a document and how often each one appears. Aura gives you a small set of collection types for holding those groups, and if you've written Python they will look familiar. A `list[T]` keeps values in order. A `dict[K, V]` maps keys to values. A `set[T]` holds each value once. `str`, which you've been using since the first chapter, is a sequence of text with its own rules, and `Array[T]` is a block of numbers for arithmetic on a whole table at a time.
- [Lists](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch08-01-lists): A `list[T]` holds values of one type `T`, in order, and grows as you add to it. It's the collection you'll reach for most, so it's where we'll start our gradebook: one student's scores on a run of assignments.
- [Strings](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch08-02-strings): Our gradebook's data will arrive as text, one student per line:
- [Dictionaries and sets](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch08-03-dicts-and-sets): A list answers "what's at position 3?". Most questions a gradebook asks are different: "what are Grace's scores?", "has Alan handed anything in?". For questions by name, you want a `dict[K, V]`, which maps keys of type `K` to values of type `V`. For questions of membership alone, you want a `set[T]`. Both work much as they do in Python, and both follow the ownership rules of the last section, with one twist for keys that's worth slowing down for.
- [Comprehensions and builtins](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch08-04-comprehensions-and-builtins): By now our gradebook code has a lot of loops that look the same: make an empty collection, walk another one, maybe test something, append. Python programmers write most of those as comprehensions, and Aura has the same syntax for lists, sets, and dictionaries. It also has the builtins you'd reach for next, such as `sum`, `max`, and `sorted`, so that a question like "what's the best score in the class?" takes one line instead of five.
- [Numeric arrays](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch08-05-numeric-arrays): Our gradebook is really a table: one row per student, one column per assignment, a number in every cell. We've been storing it as a dictionary of lists, which is flexible, and that flexibility costs something. Each list is its own allocation, each row can have a different length, and every calculation is a loop we write by hand. When the data is a rectangular table of numbers and the work is arithmetic, Aura has a type built for it: `Array[T]`.
- [Error handling](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch09-00-error-handling): Programs fail. A file is missing, a user types `80a` where a port number should be, a loop reads one element past the end of a list. Python treats all of these the same way: something raises an exception, the exception travels up the call stack until a `try` block catches it, and if nothing catches it the program prints a traceback and exits. That model is convenient to write, but a reader looking at a function call cannot tell whether it might raise, or what it might raise, without reading every function it calls.
- [Traps: failures that stop a task](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch09-01-traps): Our settings loader starts out with a hopeful view of its input. Every line of a settings file should look like `port = 9000`: a key, an equals sign, a value. So the first version splits each line on `=` and takes the two halves. Create a file called `src/main.au` (in a new package from `aura new settings`, or anywhere you like) and type this in:
- [Recoverable errors with `Result`](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors): When `parse_line` meets a line without `=`, the right response depends on who is asking. A command-line tool should print a helpful message and exit with a non-zero status. An editor plugin should underline the line. A server reloading its configuration should keep the old settings and log a warning. `parse_line` can't know which of these it's part of, so it shouldn't decide. Its job is to say what went wrong and hand that answer back.
- [To trap or not to trap](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch09-03-to-trap-or-not): You now have two ways for a function to fail. It can trap, which ends the task with a diagnostic, or it can return `Result.Err`, which hands the problem to its caller. Neither is better in general. Each one makes a different promise, and choosing well is mostly a matter of asking one question about the failure: whose mistake is it?
- [Generics, traits, and conversions](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch10-00-generics-traits-conversions): Every program eventually grows two functions that are the same except for a type. One finds the largest `int64` in a list, the other the largest `str`. One stack holds undo actions, another holds numbers. Copying the code works for a while, and then a bug gets fixed in one copy and not the other. Python avoids the problem by not checking types until the program runs, so one function can accept anything and fail later if the thing doesn't support what the function does with it. Aura checks types before the program runs, so it needs a way to write code once and still say exactly what that code requires.
- [Generic functions and classes](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch10-01-generics): Let's start with the duplication problem in its plainest form. Here are two functions that find the largest value in a list, one for integers and one for strings:
- [Traits](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch10-02-traits): A trait names a set of methods that a type can promise to provide. Code that works with "any type that has these methods" asks for the trait, and the compiler checks the promise on both sides: that each type claiming the trait really has the methods, and that generic code only calls methods the trait provides. If you've used Python's abstract base classes, Go's interfaces, or Rust's traits, the idea will be familiar. The Aura version is closest to Rust's.
- [Converting between types](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch10-03-conversions): In Python, `2 + 0.5` is `2.5`, `len(items) / 2` is a float, and an integer quietly grows as large as it needs to be. Aura does none of these things. A value keeps its type until you write a conversion, and every conversion you write either produces an exact result, traps, or returns a `Result`. This section shows the three tools for numbers and text, explains why Aura is this strict, and ends with conversions between your own types.
- [Writing automated tests](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch11-00-testing): By now the compiler checks a great deal for you. It knows every value's type, it knows who owns what, and it won't let you reach the inside of a `Result` without handling the error. What it can't know is what you meant. If a function is supposed to apply a 10% discount and it applies 1%, the types are perfect and the program is wrong. Tests are how you write down what you meant, so a machine can check it every time the code changes.
- [How to write tests](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch11-01-writing-tests): Tests live in a package, so we begin with an empty one. `aura new` creates it, and as you saw in [Chapter 1](/book/ch01-03-hello-packages), it already includes a place for tests:
- [Running tests and reading failures](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch11-02-running-tests): A test suite is only as useful as its output is readable. When something fails at the end of a long day, you want to know which case failed, where, and with what values, without scrolling. This section looks closely at what `aura test` prints, what happens when the code under test traps instead of failing an assertion, and how to run only the tests you care about right now.
- [Organizing tests](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch11-03-organizing-tests): A handful of tests fits comfortably in one file. A real package collects hundreds, some fast and pure, some that touch files or start processes, some that run the same check over a table of inputs. Keeping that collection readable takes four things from the runner: a way to split tests across files, a way to generate cases from a list, output a CI system can read, and setup that runs around each case.
- [An I/O project: building a log analyzer](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch12-00-log-analyzer): Every service you run writes a log, and sooner or later someone asks a question the log can answer: how many errors came in overnight, which service produced them, whether the noise is coming from one place or from everywhere. In this chapter we'll build `logscan`, a small command-line tool that reads a log file and prints a report answering those questions. It is the kind of program people write in an afternoon with a shell pipeline of `grep`, `awk`, and `sort`, and then rewrite when the pipeline stops fitting on one line.
- [Reading the arguments and the file](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch12-01-reading-input): As always, we start with a new package:
- [Parsing lines into records](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch12-02-parsing-records): At the end of the last section `run` held a list of lines, each one a plain `str`. We could count errors straight from those strings with `line.contains("ERROR")`, and for a one-off question that would be fine. But "contains `ERROR`" also matches a message like `retrying after ERROR from upstream`, it can't tell us which service a line came from, and every new question would mean another round of string poking. It is better to read each line once, at the edge of the program, and turn it into a value whose type says exactly what a log entry is. After that the rest of the program works with types instead of text, and the compiler can check it.
- [Aggregating and reporting](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch12-03-aggregating): `run` can now turn every line into a `Record` or a `None`. What we want from `logscan` is not a list of records, though, but a summary: how many records there were at each level, how many came from each service, which services produced the errors, and which lines we had to skip. In this section we'll collect those numbers in one value as the records stream past, and then print them as a small aligned report.
- [Refactoring with tests and better errors](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch12-04-refactoring-with-tests): `logscan` works, and it is the kind of program that tends to stay in one file long after it should have been split up. The trouble with one file is not its length. It is that every part can reach every other part, so nothing can be checked on its own. To find out whether `parse_line` handles a lowercase level, we would have to write a log file, run the whole program, and read the report.
- [Closures and decorators](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch13-00-closures-and-decorators): So far, the functions in this book have been things we call. In this chapter they become things we pass around. A sort that should order requests by duration needs to be told how to get the duration out of a request. A filter that keeps "requests slower than the limit the user typed" needs to carry that limit with it. A tool runner that should log every call needs a way to put the same logging around many different functions without editing each one.
- [Closures](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch13-01-closures): Let's start from a question we could ask of the log in the last chapter: which requests were slow? Suppose we already have the durations, in milliseconds, in a list. Finding the slow ones is a filter, and a list's `filter` method takes a function that says yes or no for each element.
- [Decorators](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch13-02-decorators): The last section ended with `slower_than`, a function that took a limit and returned a closure built around it. Now suppose the thing we hand in is not a number but another function, and what we get back is a new function that does a little extra work around each call to the old one: print a trace line, count the calls, retry on failure. Writing that by hand at every place we define a function would be tedious and easy to forget. A *decorator* does it once, at the definition.
- [Resources and cleanup](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch14-00-resources-and-cleanup): Programs hold on to things that belong to the outside world. An open file is a slot in the operating system's file table. A socket is a connection that the machine on the other end is keeping alive for us. A temporary file sits on disk until somebody deletes it. Each of these has to be given back, and the hard part is not remembering to give it back on the happy path. The hard part is giving it back when the function returns early, when an error propagates out through `try`, or when a trap stops the task halfway through.
- [`with` and deterministic cleanup](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch14-01-with-and-cleanup): Let's start with a small, ordinary job: count the lines in a text file. Make a new package with `aura new line_count`, put a `notes.txt` with three lines next to `Aura.toml`, and replace `src/main.au` with this:
- [Writing your own resource manager](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch14-02-resource-managers): The standard library's resources close themselves, but plenty of cleanup is specific to your program. A test fixture deletes the directory it set up. A progress bar erases itself when the work is done. A transaction rolls back if it was never committed. In Aura, any class can take part in `with` by following a small protocol, and once it does, it gets the same guarantees as `fs.File`.
- [Structured concurrency](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch15-00-concurrency): Sooner or later a program needs to do more than one thing at a time. A server handles many connections. A build tool compiles several files at once. A crawler waits on dozens of slow network requests and would like to do something useful while it waits. Concurrency is how a program overlaps that work, and it has a reputation for producing the worst bugs in software: work that keeps running after everyone has forgotten it, failures that vanish because nobody was listening, two pieces of code changing the same data at the same moment.
- [Tasks and task groups](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch15-01-tasks-and-task-groups): A *task* is a function call that runs concurrently with the code that started it. Tasks are lightweight: each has its own small stack, and the Aura runtime schedules thousands of them over a handful of operating system threads. You never create a task on its own. You ask a `TaskGroup` to start one, and the group is responsible for it from then on.
- [Passing work with queues](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch15-02-queues): In the last section every task got all of its input when it started and handed back one value when it finished. Plenty of concurrent programs don't fit that shape. A producer reads lines from a file and wants to hand each one off as soon as it has it. A logger receives messages from many tasks for as long as the program runs. For work that flows between tasks while they run, Aura has `Queue[T]`: a typed channel that one task puts values into and another takes them out of.
- [Cancellation, timeouts, and shutdown](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch15-03-cancellation-and-shutdown): Starting work is the easy half of concurrency. The hard half is stopping it: giving up on a task that's taking too long, shutting down a pool when the job is done, and making sure that whatever was running gets to clean up on the way out. This section is about that half. We'll see that a timeout and a cancellation are different things, how a task notices that it's been cancelled, and what a task group does at the end of its block when some of its tasks are still waiting.
- [A worker pool](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch15-04-worker-pool): We now have every piece we need for the most common shape in concurrent programs: a pool of workers. One task produces jobs. Several workers take jobs from a shared queue, process them, and send results to a second queue. The parent collects the results and decides when the whole thing is finished. The same shape runs build systems, web crawlers, and image converters, and in [Chapter 19](/book/ch19-00-final-project) we'll use it for a job runner.
- [Talking to the world](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch16-00-talking-to-the-world): Every program we have written so far has lived inside its own process. It computed something, printed it, and stopped. Real tools spend most of their time on the edges: they read configuration from disk, start other programs, make HTTP requests, and write results somewhere another program can pick them up. Those edges are where things go wrong in ways your code does not control. A file is missing, a command hangs, a server refuses the connection, a JSON document has a typo in line 40.
- [Files and the filesystem](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch16-01-files): Let's start `checkup` the way most tools start: by reading a file somebody else wrote. Create the package:
- [Running processes and supervisors](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch16-02-processes): A health checker that can only look for files is not very healthy. The most flexible check is "run this command and tell me whether it worked", because then any existing tool becomes a check: `pg_isready`, `systemctl is-active`, a shell script your team already has. We will fill in the `Command` probe, then look at talking to a running child through pipes, and finish with supervisors, which keep a set of children alive under a restart policy.
- [Networking and HTTP](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch16-03-networking): The third probe in `checkup` asks a question over the network: does this URL answer, and with what status? Before we write it, we need something to check. We will build up to that in two steps. First we write a tiny TCP server and client in one program, which shows how sockets fit with tasks. Then we write a small HTTP server as its own program, and point `checkup` at it. Everything in this section runs on `127.0.0.1`, so you can follow along without internet access.
- [JSON](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch16-04-json): Two things about `checkup` are now awkward. The config format is ours, and it cannot say much: an argument with a space in it cannot be written, because we split on whitespace, and every new option would mean more parsing code. The report is text meant for people, so a dashboard or a CI job that wants to know which checks failed has to parse `name: detail` lines and hope nobody puts a colon in a name. JSON fixes both. It is the format other tools already read and write, and Aura's `json` module can convert between JSON text and your own classes and enums, with errors that name the field that was wrong.
- [Building, debugging, and shipping](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch17-00-shipping): Up to now every program in this book has been started with `aura run`. That is the right command while you are writing code: it checks the program and runs it in one step, with nothing left behind on disk. But a tool is not finished until it runs somewhere else, on a server or in a CI job or on a colleague's laptop, without the compiler and without its source code.
- [`aura run` vs `aura build`, and what a native binary contains](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch17-01-run-and-build): Aura has two ways to execute a program, and you have been using one of them without having to think about it. Both start the same way. The compiler reads your source and every module it imports, checks types and ownership, and lowers the result to MIR, the compiler's mid-level intermediate representation. MIR is a simplified form of the program in which every borrow, move, and drop is explicit. What happens next is the difference.
- [Debugging in VS Code](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch17-02-debugging): When a program misbehaves, the first question is "where?" and the second is "what were the values?". Aura answers the first one for free in most cases, and a debug build plus a debugger answers the second. We will start with what you already have, then build `scores` from the previous section for a debugger and step through it, first in plain lldb so you can see exactly what is happening, and then in VS Code, where the same thing is one key press.
- [Performance](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch17-03-performance): "Is it fast?" is the wrong question about a language, because the answer depends on what your program does. The useful questions are narrower. Which operations are cheap in Aura today, and which still cost more than they would in Rust or C? How do you find out where your own program spends its time? And which published numbers can you trust? We will take them in order, and we will be careful about where every number comes from. Some come from measurements made while writing this chapter; the rest come from the Manual's [Performance](/manual/performance) page, which records each measurement with its workload, machine, compiler commit, and raw data.
- [Calling C](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch18-00-calling-c): Sooner or later you will want a function that Aura's standard modules do not have but the C library on your machine does. Most operating-system services are C functions underneath, and so are a great many libraries. Aura can call them through its foreign function interface, FFI v0. It is deliberately small: it lets you bind a handful of trusted C functions with simple signatures, and it does not let C code reach into Aura's memory in ways the compiler cannot see. This chapter shows what it can do, what it refuses to do, and why the line is where it is.
- [Final project: a supervised job runner](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch19-00-final-project): We have reached the last chapter, and it is time to put most of the book to work in one program. We are going to build `jobrunner`, a small tool that reads a list of jobs from a file, runs each one as a child process, and reports what happened. By the end it will run several jobs at once through a worker pool, retry the ones that fail under a per-job restart policy, kill jobs that run past their timeout, and shut the whole pool down cleanly when an overall deadline passes, without leaving a single stray process behind.
- [A single-task runner](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch19-01-single-task-runner): Every concurrent program starts life as a sequential one. Before we think about workers and queues, we want a runner that does one job at a time and does it correctly: it reads the job file, runs each command, captures what the command printed, and tells us plainly which jobs failed. Once that part is solid, making it parallel is a change to the shape of the program, not to what each job does.
- [Running jobs in parallel with a worker pool](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch19-02-worker-pool): The single-task runner spends most of its life waiting. While `nap` sleeps, the runner sits in `process.run` doing nothing, and every job behind it in the file waits too. Let's make that cost visible before we fix it. Here is a job file with three one-second naps:
- [Supervision, restarts, and graceful shutdown](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/ch19-03-supervision-and-shutdown): The pool from the last section runs jobs quickly, but it assumes every job behaves. Real jobs do not. A deploy step fails because a server was briefly unreachable, and would have passed a second later. A test hangs on a lock and never exits. Somebody kicks off the runner at the end of the day and needs it to stop after ten minutes no matter what. A runner that cannot handle these cases is one you end up babysitting.
- [Appendices](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/appendix-00-appendices): The appendices are reference material, meant for looking things up rather than reading straight through. Each one gathers in one place something the main chapters introduced a piece at a time.
- [Appendix A: Keywords](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/appendix-01-keywords): This appendix lists the words Aura's lexer treats specially. Most of them are *reserved*: you cannot use them as the name of a binding, a parameter, a function, or a field. A handful more are *contextual*: they are ordinary identifiers almost everywhere, and take on a special meaning only in one position. The [Lexical structure](/manual/lexical-structure) page of the Manual has the exact rules.
- [Appendix B: Operators and symbols](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/appendix-02-operators): This appendix collects Aura's operators and the punctuation that carries meaning in its syntax. If you know Python, almost all of it will look familiar, and the differences are deliberate: Aura has no implicit numeric conversion, no truthiness, and no integer `/`, because each of those is a place where Python quietly picks an answer for you. The [Expressions](/manual/expressions) page of the Manual has the full typing and evaluation rules.
- [Appendix C: Aura for Python developers](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/appendix-03-from-python): Aura was designed so that Python programmers would feel at home in it, and on the surface they do. Blocks are indented, functions start with `def`, classes with `class`, strings with f-strings work the way you expect, and so do comprehensions, keyword arguments, `for x in items`, `with`, and chained comparisons. That familiarity is useful, but it also means the differences arrive as surprises: code that looks right and does not compile. This appendix collects those differences in one place, with the reason for each, so that the first week with Aura is less of a negotiation with the compiler.
- [Appendix D: Useful tools](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/appendix-04-tools): The `aura` command does more than compile and run programs. It formats code, runs tests, generates API documentation, and powers the editor support in VS Code. This appendix is a tour of those tools, in roughly the order you will want them. The [CLI and tooling](/manual/cli-and-tooling) page of the Manual lists every command and flag.
- [Appendix E: Diagnostics you will meet often](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/book/appendix-05-common-diagnostics): Every message `aura` prints starts with a stable code such as `AU3001`. The first digit after `AU` tells you which part of the compiler is talking: `1` for reading the text of your program, `2` for names and types, `3` for ownership and borrowing, and `4` for traps at run time. The code stays the same from release to release even when the wording improves, so it is the thing to search for.

## Learn Aura

- [Learn Aura](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn): This book teaches Aura through short programs that do something real. Each chapter extends them until the pieces fit together.
- [Converting Between Types](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/casting): Aura never converts a number for you. An `int32` does not become an `int64` on its own, and an integer does not turn into a float. You write every conversion, and there are three ways to write one.
- [Working With Collections](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/collections): Aura has three collection types: `list[T]`, `dict[K, V]`, and `set[T]`. Each one holds a single static element type. Ownership of the elements is deterministic, and lookups report absence explicitly.
- [Structured Concurrency](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/concurrency): This page covers structured concurrency in Aura. Every task starts inside a scope, and leaving that scope waits for, cancels, or otherwise accounts for its children. Child work with no parent is hard to reason about. A task started deep inside a function might run forever, fail silently, or leak a resource.
- [Shaping Data](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/data-modeling): This page shows how to give your data names and pick the right shape for it. A loose bag of strings and integers becomes a `Job` with an `id`, a `queue`, and an `attempts` counter. A value that is sometimes a number and sometimes an error becomes a `Result` with two variants. Shared behavior lives on the type.
- [Calling A Small C API](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/ffi): Aura's Foreign Function Interface (FFI) v0 is for small, reviewed bindings to trusted C symbols that are already visible in the running process. It does not expose raw pointers or arbitrary library loading.
- [Aura For Python Developers](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/from-python): Most of what you know from Python carries over. Indentation, `def`, `class`, f-strings, comprehensions, keyword arguments, and `for x in items` all work the way you expect. This page covers the parts that differ, so the compiler stops surprising you.
- [Getting Aura Running](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/install-and-run): This chapter installs Aura, runs a first program, and builds a native binary. It covers both a release archive and a source checkout.
- [Talking To The World](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/io-process-networking): This chapter covers the four built-in modules that reach outside the program:
- [Organizing Code](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/modules-and-packages): This page takes a program from a single file to a package with dependencies. A single file is a fine place to start. As a program grows, helper types need a home, public APIs need marking, and dependencies need a place where the compiler can read them. Aura's modules and packages cover all three.
- [Running And Shipping](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/native-builds): Aura has two execution paths. `aura run` uses the MIR runtime, and `aura build` uses the native code generator. MIR is Aura's mid-level intermediate representation. Both paths target the same language surface, and the same test suite exercises both. They suit different moments in a project.
- [Values, Moves, And Borrows](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/ownership-and-borrowing): This is the central chapter of the book. Most of Aura follows from the rules here: how functions receive data, how collections hold it, how tasks share it, and how resources get cleaned up.
- [Results And Optional Values](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/results-and-options): Values can be absent, and operations can fail. Aura puts both facts in the type system, so the code shows which calls can go wrong and how.
- [The First Program](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/small-programs): This chapter builds a small classifier. It takes a list of numbers, sorts each one into a category, counts how often each category appears, and prints a report.
- [Testing](https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/learn/testing): The compiler checks ownership and failure, but it cannot tell you whether your logic is right. Tests do that. Aura ships its own test runner, so you do not need to pick one.

## Tutorials

- [Overview](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/00-overview.md): These tutorials teach Aura as the compiler in this repository implements it today. They do not teach proposed features that are not built yet.
- [Running Programs](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/01-running-programs.md): You run Aura programs with the `aura` command-line interface (CLI). From a source checkout, invoke it from the repository root with `cargo run -p aura --`.
- [Bindings And Types](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/02-bindings-and-types.md): Every Aura value has a type known at compile time. You create a binding with plain assignment. There is no `let` keyword.
- [Functions](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/03-functions.md): You declare a function with `def`. Every parameter needs an explicit type.
- [Control Flow](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/04-control-flow.md): This chapter covers conditionals, comparisons, loops, early exit, and comprehensions. Pattern matching with `match` has its own chapter, [09-enums-and-match.md](09-enums-and-match.md).
- [Classes And Data](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/05-classes-and-data.md): This chapter shows how to declare a class, construct and read its values, and give it methods. It also covers default values, visibility, copy classes, and recursive fields.
- [Ownership And Borrowing](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/06-ownership-and-borrowing.md): If you are coming from Python, this is the most important chapter in the tutorial. Aura has no garbage collector. It tracks who owns each value and when that value can be freed. This tracking is called ownership. Lending a value for a while without giving it away is called borrowing.
- [Strings And Numbers](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/07-strings-and-numbers.md): This chapter covers arithmetic, the numeric types and conversions between them, numeric arrays, strings, parsing, formatting, booleans, and `Duration` values.
- [Tooling](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/08-tooling.md): This chapter covers the tools that ship in the Aura monorepo: the `aura` command-line interface (CLI), the example library, and the VS Code extension.
- [Enums And Match](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/09-enums-and-match.md): An enum is a type whose value is one of several named variants. `match` picks an arm by variant, and the compiler checks that the arms cover every case. This chapter also shows how `match` and `is None` work on union types such as `int64 | str | None`.
- [Results And Optional Values](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/10-results-and-options.md): Aura handles recoverable errors with values, not exceptions. This chapter covers the four types involved:
- [Resource Management](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/11-resource-management.md): A `with` statement runs a block with one or more context managers and exits each one when the block ends. Use it for files, network connections, task groups, and your own classes. The exit runs whether the block finishes normally or leaves early. It works like Python's `with` statement and context managers.
- [Error Propagation](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/12-error-propagation.md): `try expr` passes an error up to the caller so you do not have to write a `match` for every fallible call. This chapter shows how it works and where you can use it.
- [Concurrency](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/13-concurrency.md): Aura runs concurrent code as lightweight tasks. Every task belongs to a `TaskGroup`, and tasks pass values to each other through typed queues. This chapter covers queues, task groups, task results, waiting on several sources, cancellation, and how the scheduler runs tasks.
- [Current Language Surface](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/14-current-language-surface.md): This chapter is a reference for the part of Aura that the compiler supports today. Learn the language from the earlier chapters, then use this page to check whether a form, type, or library call is available.
- [Generics](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/15-generics.md): A generic definition takes type parameters, so one `Box[T]` works across every type that meets its requirements. You do not need separate `BoxInt`, `BoxString`, and `BoxFloat` classes.
- [Traits](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/16-traits.md): A trait names behavior that different types can implement. Traits play the role of Python's abstract base classes or Go's interfaces. Code written against a trait works with any type that provides the trait's methods.
- [Modules And Visibility](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/17-modules-and-visibility.md): This chapter shows how to split a program across files. A module is one local `.au` file. You bring it in with `import` or `from ... import ...`, and you choose what it exposes with `public`.
- [Packages And Workspaces](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/18-packages-and-workspaces.md): This chapter covers Aura's package system. A package is a directory with an `Aura.toml` manifest and a `src/` directory. Packages can depend on local paths and git repositories, and a workspace groups several packages under one root.
- [I/O And Networking](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/19-io-and-networking.md): This chapter covers terminal, file, process, and network I/O. Four builtin modules provide it:
- [Deterministic And Secure Randomness](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/20-randomness.md): Aura has two kinds of randomness, and you pick the one whose promise you need:
- [Working With JSON Values](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/21-json.md): This chapter shows how to parse, inspect, build, and dump JSON. The `json` module parses untrusted text into its own recursive value type and reports failures as typed errors you can recover from. Its output is deterministic, so you can use it for service messages, fixtures, and cache keys.
- [Bytes, Encodings, And Hashes](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/22-bytes.md): Aura represents raw bytes as `list[uint8]`. File, socket, process, and secure-random byte APIs all return that same type, so bytes pass between them with no wrapper conversion.
- [Assertions And Tests](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/23-assertions-and-tests.md): An assertion states a condition that must hold. If the condition is false, the program fails at once and the failure points to the source line. Use the short form when the default message is enough:
- [Multiline Expressions](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/24-multiline-expressions.md): You can split one logical expression across several physical lines. The rule is short: a line continues while a `(`, `[`, or `{` is still open.
- [Tuples](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/25-tuples.md): A tuple bundles a fixed number of values, which may have different types. Use one when a function has two or three natural results and a class would add more ceremony than meaning.
- [26. Foreign Function Interface v0](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/26-ffi.md): Aura's foreign function interface, FFI v0, binds small, trusted C APIs. It does not open the language to general pointer manipulation. Only a package can declare FFI functions, and its manifest must opt in explicitly.
- [Typed Tool Agents](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/27-typed-tool-agents.md): This chapter builds the core of a tool-calling agent. A model sends a tool call as JSON text. The program checks the arguments against a typed class, runs the tool, and sends back a JSON result. Three features do the work:
- [Aura Tutorials](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/tutorials/README.md): These chapters teach Aura as the compiler in this repository implements it today. Read them in order, like a book. Each chapter introduces one part of the language and shows runnable code.
